How this book matches your exam. This book follows the 2027–2029 syllabus (first exams 2027). It covers Topic 1, Changing river environments, which is tested in Paper 1: Physical Geography. Paper 1 lasts 1 hour 45 minutes, carries 75 marks and is worth 36% of the qualification. It has two sections:

  • Section A: one compulsory 25-mark question.
  • Section B: you answer two of three 25-mark questions.

Geographical skills are now tested in every paper, so each unit includes data and diagram practice. The syllabus asks for two detailed examples in this topic: a named river flood and a named river pollution example. This book uses the 2022 Indus floods in Pakistan and pollution of the Ganga in India. Facts were checked against published sources. The marking guides are our own, not official Cambridge mark schemes.

Unit 1 of 10: The Drainage Basin and the Water Cycle

Key ideas

  • A drainage basin is the area of land drained by a river and its tributaries.
  • Features of a drainage basin:
  • Watershed: the high ground that forms the edge of the basin.
  • Source: where the river starts.
  • Mouth: where the river meets the sea or a lake.
  • Tributary: a smaller river that joins a larger one.
  • Confluence: the point where two rivers join.
  • The basin as an open system:
  • Inputs: precipitation.
  • Stores: interception (on plants), surface storage, soil water, groundwater and the river channel.
  • Flows (transfers): infiltration, percolation, surface runoff (overland flow), throughflow and groundwater flow.
  • Outputs: evaporation, transpiration (together called evapotranspiration) and river discharge.

Worked examples

Example 1: heavy rain falls on dry, baked ground. Infiltration is slow, so surface runoff increases and water reaches the river quickly.

Example 2: a forested basin has high interception and transpiration, so less water reaches the river.

Example 3: water that soaks deep into permeable rock moves slowly to the river as groundwater flow. This keeps the river flowing in dry weather. This steady supply is called baseflow.

10-mark exam-style question

(a) Define watershed and confluence. [2]

(b) Distinguish between infiltration and percolation. [2]

(c) Explain how deforestation in a drainage basin can increase the amount of water reaching a river. [4]

(d) Name one store and one output of the drainage basin system. [2]

Answers:

  • (a) The watershed is the boundary of high ground around a drainage basin (B1). A confluence is where two rivers meet (B1).
  • (b) Infiltration is water soaking into the soil from the surface (B1). Percolation is water moving down from the soil into the rock below (B1).
  • (c) Award up to 4 marks:
  • there is less interception by leaves (B1);
  • there is less transpiration (B1);
  • more water runs off the surface because roots no longer hold the soil open, and the soil becomes compacted (B1);
  • so water reaches the river faster and in larger amounts (B1).
  • (d) Store: soil water, groundwater, interception or surface storage (B1). Output: evaporation, transpiration or river discharge (B1).

Common mistakes

  1. Mixing up infiltration and percolation.
  2. Calling transpiration an input.
  3. Describing the watershed as "where water is collected".
  4. Saying "more rain" when the question asks about land use.
  5. Leaving out the effect on the river in a "how" or "why" answer.

Quick recall

  1. What is the main input to a drainage basin?
  2. What is water flowing sideways through the soil called?
  3. What is the edge of a drainage basin called?
  4. Is interception a store or a flow?
  5. What is the combined name for evaporation and transpiration?

Answers: 1) Precipitation. 2) Throughflow. 3) The watershed. 4) A store. 5) Evapotranspiration.
